mitigations: Implement token-based authentication (JWT / OAuth2)
Validate identity at every trust boundary crossing
Reject unauthenticated requests at the entry point
threats.threat_context: The user component lacks authentication enforcement at a trust boundary crossing on dataflow df9, meaning any request originating from this component is not cryptographically or session-validated before being accepted by downstream agentic components. An attacker can impersonate a legitimate user by injecting or replaying unauthenticated requests across this boundary, causing the AI agent to execute actions, access data, or trigger workflows under a falsely assumed identity. In an agentic-AI architecture this is critical because agents often perform autonomous, chained actions with elevated privileges, so a single spoofed boundary crossing can cascade into unauthorized data exfiltration, resource manipulation, or compromise of the entire agent execution pipeline.

In an agentic AI architecture this is critical because unauthenticated user inputs can propagate through autonomous agent chains, causing cascading unauthorized actions, data exfiltration, or privilege escalation with no verified accountability trail.

mitigations: Route all external traffic through an API gateway or load balancer

threats.threat_context: The llm-reason component, which handles core reasoning and inference logic, is directly reachable from an untrusted network zone without an intervening trust boundary or authentication layer, meaning an attacker can send crafted inputs directly to the reasoning engine without passing through any gatekeeping controls. An attacker could exploit this by submitting malicious prompts, adversarial inputs, or forged identity tokens directly to llm-reason, bypassing prompt filtering, rate limiting, or session validation that would normally be enforced at a higher-trust boundary. This is critical because the reasoning component is the decision-making core of the agentic system - direct untrusted access allows an adversary to manipulate agent behavior, inject false context, or impersonate trusted orchestrators, potentially compromising every downstream action the agent takes.

threats.subcategory: Unvalidated Input to Data Store - Data Poisoning Risk
threats.description: 'vector-store' (vector-store) accepts data from 'environment' (low trust) via flow 'df10' without input validation. An attacker can manipulate this data to compromise AI agent behavior, leading to biased results or unintended consequences in AI decision making - a data poisoning attack.
mitigations: Validate and sanitize all data before writing to AI data stores
Implement provenance tracking - record the source of all stored data

threats.threat_context: The vector store accepts embeddings or raw text inputs without validation, meaning an attacker who can influence upstream data pipelines or directly submit content can inject semantically crafted vectors designed to corrupt retrieval results or bias the AI agent's context window. Exploitation involves inserting poisoned documents or manipulated embedding vectors that cause the retrieval system to surface attacker-controlled content during similarity searches, effectively hijacking the agent's grounding data without altering the model itself. This is critical in agentic architectures because the vector store serves as the agent's external memory and knowledge base, meaning poisoned entries directly influence downstream reasoning, tool selection, and action execution across every query that retrieves that corrupted data.

threats.threat_context: The vector-store component accepts and indexes data from untrusted or unvalidated sources into the RAG pipeline, meaning an attacker can inject malicious, poisoned, or adversarially crafted embeddings and documents directly into the knowledge base without integrity checks. Once poisoned content is stored, any retrieval operation will surface attacker-controlled data as authoritative context to the LLM, enabling prompt injection, misinformation propagation, or manipulation of downstream agent decisions at scale. This is critical because the vector-store is the foundational trust anchor for all RAG-augmented responses, and compromising it undermines the integrity of every query served by the agentic system.

attack_paths.name: Initial Access via user -> Execution on llm-reason

steps.threat_subcategory: No Access Controls on Infrastructure - Orchestration Attack Risk

attack_paths.attack_story: This is a critical-severity attack path that exploits a complete absence of authentication controls from the public boundary all the way into the AI reasoning core. An attacker requires no valid credentials or identity verification to enter the system - they simply cross the user boundary unchallenged and submit queries directly to an internet-facing component that performs no authentication checks. Because this unauthenticated access flows without interruption into the LLM reasoning layer, the attacker arrives at the orchestration engine with full interaction capability. Once inside the llm-reason component, the absence of access controls on the infrastructure means the attacker can invoke AI agent tools directly, turning the reasoning layer into an execution environment under their control. The path from anonymous external user to unrestricted AI orchestration is completely unobstructed.

step_walkthrough.threat_explanation: At this step, the attacker crosses the user-facing boundary of the system without any authentication challenge - no login, no token, no identity verification is enforced (MITRE Initial Access: Valid Accounts exploitation via Unauthenticated Boundary Crossing). This means any anonymous actor on the internet can enter the system as if they were a legitimate user. There is no gate to stop them.

The attacker's unauthenticated request reaches the query component, which is directly internet-facing and applies no authentication controls of its own (MITRE Initial Access: Valid Accounts, Unauthenticated Internet-Facing Component). This compounds Step 1 - not only did the boundary fail to block the attacker, but the query interface also performs no validation of who is submitting requests. The attacker can craft and submit arbitrary queries with no restriction.

The unauthenticated, adversary-controlled query now reaches the llm-reason component - the AI reasoning and orchestration engine (MITRE Execution: AI Agent Tool Invocation). Because there are no access controls on this infrastructure, the attacker can directly invoke AI agent tools. Concretely, this means they can trigger downstream tool calls, manipulate the reasoning pipeline, exfiltrate data surfaced by the agent, inject malicious instructions into the orchestration flow, abuse any connected APIs or data sources the agent has access to, and potentially use the agent as a pivot point to reach other systems it is authorized to interact with.

attack_paths.business_impact: An unauthenticated attacker with unrestricted access to your AI reasoning and orchestration layer can manipulate the outputs your customers and employees receive, inject false or harmful content into AI-driven workflows, and abuse connected systems - exposing your organization to severe reputational damage, loss of customer trust, and regulatory scrutiny under frameworks such as the EU AI Act, GDPR, and NIST AI RMF, which mandate demonstrable controls over AI system access and integrity.

attack_paths.name: Initial Access via tools -> Execution on llm-reason

steps.threat_subcategory: No Access Controls on Infrastructure - Orchestration Attack Risk

attack_paths.attack_story: An attacker gains entry through the tools component by exploiting valid, legitimate credentials - bypassing authentication entirely rather than breaking it. Because neither the tools nor the environment components have logging in place, this lateral movement goes completely undetected as the attacker advances from tools into the execution environment. The absence of access controls on the LLM reasoning component then allows the attacker to invoke AI agent tools directly, without any orchestration-level checks standing in their way. This chain succeeds not because of a single catastrophic flaw, but because three consecutive components share the same blind spots: no visibility and no enforcement. By the time the attacker reaches the LLM reasoning layer, they have full, uncontested influence over how the AI agent thinks and acts.

step_walkthrough.threat_explanation: Using valid account credentials - likely stolen, reused, or left unrotated - the attacker authenticates to the tools component as a trusted user. Under MITRE tactic Initial Access via the Valid Accounts technique, this means no alarm is raised and no authentication failure is logged. Critically, because this component is internet-facing with no logging, there is no audit trail of who accessed it, when, or from where. The attacker is invisible from the moment they walk in.

Carrying the same or inherited credentials, the attacker pivots from the tools component into the execution environment - again using Valid Accounts under the Initial Access tactic. This step is possible because the environment component shares the same weakness: it is internet-facing and produces no logs. This means the lateral movement between steps 1 and 2 is not just undetected - it is undetectable after the fact, eliminating any forensic opportunity to reconstruct the intrusion.

Now inside the environment, the attacker reaches the LLM reasoning component, which has no access controls on its infrastructure. Under the Execution tactic using the AI Agent Tool Invocation technique, the attacker can directly invoke tools through the AI agent without any orchestration-level gate or identity check stopping them. At this point the attacker can manipulate the reasoning outputs of the AI agent - injecting false context, altering decisions the agent makes on behalf of users, triggering unintended tool calls, exfiltrating data that the agent has access to through its tool integrations, or causing the agent to take destructive actions within the systems it is connected to.

attack_paths.business_impact: Because the compromised LLM reasoning component directly shapes outputs visible to end users and downstream systems, any manipulation of its behavior - whether to spread false information, make flawed decisions, or expose sensitive data - carries serious reputational damage and potential regulatory exposure under frameworks such as the EU AI Act, GDPR, and SOC 2, where auditability and integrity of automated decision-making are explicit requirements.

attack_paths.name: Initial Access via response -> Execution on llm-reason

steps.threat_subcategory: No Access Controls on Infrastructure - Orchestration Attack Risk

additional_risks.risk: In an agentic architecture where the LLM reasoning component both plans and selects tools, a prompt injection embedded in retrieved vector-store content or tool outputs can hijack the agent's reasoning loop, causing it to chain unintended tool calls or exfiltrate data across multiple autonomous steps. Because the LLM cannot distinguish between its instructions and adversarial content injected mid-pipeline, a single poisoned retrieval result can cascade into full agent goal hijacking.
additional_risks.suggested_mitigation: Implement a structured output schema with a sandboxed instruction parser that separates system-level directives from retrieved or tool-returned content, and enforce a cryptographically signed instruction boundary so only the originating orchestrator can issue new goal directives to the reasoning loop.

additional_risks.risk: The tools component, invoked autonomously by the LLM reasoning layer, likely shares a single execution identity or credential set across all tool invocations, meaning a compromised or manipulated tool call can laterally access resources intended for other tool functions without any per-action authorization check. This over-privileged tool executor pattern turns any successful prompt injection or logic manipulation into a privilege escalation path across the environment.
additional_risks.suggested_mitigation: Enforce least-privilege per-tool credentials using short-lived, scoped tokens issued at invocation time by an intermediary authorization service, and require explicit capability declarations per tool that are validated against an allowlist before each LLM-directed call.

additional_risks.risk: With two vector-store instances present in the architecture, there is a design-level risk of inconsistent retrieval trust boundaries where one store may serve external or user-contributed embeddings while the other serves curated internal knowledge, but the llm-reason component treats both as equally authoritative sources without differentiation. This symmetric trust assignment allows attacker-influenced embeddings from the less-trusted store to override or contaminate reasoning grounded in the trusted store.
additional_risks.suggested_mitigation: Tag all retrieved chunks with a provenance trust tier at embedding time and enforce retrieval-time trust context propagation so the LLM reasoning component applies differential weighting and explicit source attribution, refusing to use lower-trust store content for security-sensitive decision branches.
